what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Maps show what to build and where markets exist
sections.para: Since 2022 I have said Wardley maps changed how I think, and the site now holds eleven in articles, seven in a vault and five in a talk. A map is a graph with a value chain and an evolution axis, telling you what moves the needle, what to build or buy, and whether a market exists.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: A map is a value chain and chosen axis
sections.para: The two kinds of context, value chain down and evolution across, are what make a map useful, and the evolution axis is a choice. A commoditised layer is a hard sell; custom building on top of one is the market. Maps are stories, they nest, and every figure is now published as data.

sections.label: What a map is, to me
sections.line: The evolution axis is a chosen scale, not fixed
sections.para: A map's vertical axis is a value chain anchored on a user; the horizontal is evolution, using Wardley's genesis, custom built, product and commodity. A 2022 Open Security Summit talk listed eleven shifts, and a lost post proposed risk, data or governance axes. Every dot is a claim; a map you cannot be wrong about is a diagram.

sections.label: Why they are so powerful
sections.line: Maps reveal needle movement, altitude, build or buy, markets
sections.para: The weekly uses: seeing what moves the needle, spotting optimisation at the wrong altitude, deciding build or buy by column, asking whether a market exists, finding flow and attrition, naming players and where to hook, giving a common language, starting with the user, drawing many maps, and the peace of no longer carrying things in your head.

sections.label: The best of ours
sections.line: The site's best maps, each with its originating context
sections.para: The collection: the mandate stack drawn from outside and inside, the Pay after you read afternoon, the three frames of Agentic cost, Places of highest leverage, A Mac of the agent's own, and the before and after of Every mistake added a rule. Vaults add Strategy Maps' seven maps, ThreatModCon 2025's five, and Agent Desk.

sections.label: Two examples of "does the market exist"
sections.line: sgit's market sits above commodities; RiskMandate's layer moved
sections.para: Every sgit layer, storage, version control and encryption, is a commodity and a hard sell; the market is the custom building above them, which the vault serves. For RiskMandate, agents became a commodity in the last year, moving the opportunity up to agent behaviour, which is genesis and custom built everywhere.

sections.label: Reading one map, as a story
sections.line: Reading one map frame by frame tells a story
sections.para: The eight frames of the Pay after you read afternoon are read out: the meter at genesis, going live on Stripe, personas hooking the articles, versions on git, the encrypted share on a vault, the reader card, and dashed next steps. Seven questions, one picture, and a reader learns what the business is.

sections.label: A map inside a map inside a map
sections.line: Every node on a map is itself a map
sections.para: As in fractal semantic graphs, zooming into a dot makes it the anchor of a child map, placed where the dot sat on the parent's evolution axis. The figure goes three levels down: business, vault, door. It also goes up to the market. Most wrong decisions draw the right map at the wrong altitude.

sections.label: Two decks
sections.line: Two printable decks present the maps as slides
sections.para: Two decks on the site print to PDF from the browser, one slide per landscape page with nothing uploaded. Why I love Wardley maps has twelve slides explaining the technique through these maps; Reading one map walks the eight frames of the afternoon with one question per slide.

sections.label: The maps as data
sections.line: Every Wardley map on the site is one query
sections.para: Each article's graph at articles/graphs now lists its figures with file, URL, caption, kind and frames, and Wardley maps are tagged. Finding every Wardley map with context is one read of articles/graphs.json and a filter on kind. The same change added play, pause and step controls to animated maps.

sections.label: For the mapping community
sections.line: Three ideas offered to the Wardley mapping community
sections.para: The maps are source, in Mermaid's Wardley syntax or small scripts, so placements can be disputed line by line. The evolution axis as a choice deserves debate with professional mappers. Nested maps, with the dot as the next anchor, are either known practice not yet written up or an extension worth testing elsewhere.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Placements are judgements, and several claims rest on memory
sections.para: Every placement is the author's claim, not a measurement. The eleven shifts are a 2022 list, not the shorter one used now. The alternative-axis post was not found, so it is restated from memory. The market readings can be wrong when layers move, and the fractal anchoring rule is a practice, not a theorem.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: a voice memo, the linked articles and vaults
sections.para: Written from a voice memo on 12 October 2026 by the site's agent, with the argument and responsibility the author's. The maps come from the linked articles and three vaults, with only the three-altitude figure and collage new. The 2022 talk was at the Open Security Summit on 14 July 2022; the figure indexing shipped in v0.7.77.
